claims.claim: Oliver measures the epigraph's drift by counting its inverted-syntax sentences: two of them, alongside parataxis across sentence boundaries and listed parallel phrases.
A roughly seventy-page stretch of the novel is defined by the absence of a key fact that is never stated outright.
claims.quote: marked by the absence of a key detail

claims.claim: At the moment Fitz's magic returns, the narration reports only what the two men are not doing and leaves what they are doing implied.
claims.quote: we are told what they are not doing

claims.claim: Oliver argues that the withheld section trains the reader to see what is not there and to supply the connections.
claims.quote: training the reader to see what is not there

claims.claim: Farah Mendlesohn, quoted by Oliver, disputes the authority of Hobb's chapter epigraphs, calling them recollection and gossip masquerading as accurate description of the past.
claims.source: Farah Mendlesohn, Rhetorics of Fantasy (Wesleyan UP, 2008) 16, quoted verbatim in Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 63-64
claims.quote: recollection and gossip masquerading as an accurate description of the past

claims.claim: Oliver notes that chapter two opens its main text with the conjunction 'But', which violates the conventional separation of epigraph from text.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, 'History in the Margins', Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: violates the conventional separation of epigraph from text

claims.claim: Oliver records two late breaches of the epigraph convention: a chapter-20 epigraph voiced from another culture's subjective perspective, and a chapter-22 narrative intrusion into the epigraph.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, 'History in the Margins', Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: an inexplicable narrative intrusion into the epigraphs

claims.claim: Ekman and Taylor say the source line attached to a world-intrinsic epigraph tells the reader what text genres exist in the secondary world, along with naming customs, titles and social positions.
claims.source: Stefan Ekman and Audrey Isabel Taylor, 'Between World and Narrative: Fictional Epigraphs and Critical World-Building', Journal of the Fantastic in the Arts 32.2 (2021) 244-265 (author copy in DiVA)
claims.quote: Naming customs, titles, and social positions, and what text genres exist

claims.claim: Ekman and Taylor argue that a reader can determine a secondary world's generic makeup from the epigraph source lines alone, without reading the epigraph texts.
claims.source: Stefan Ekman and Audrey Isabel Taylor, JFA 32.2 (2021) 244-265
claims.quote: Even without reading the texts of the epigraphs, it is possible

claims.claim: Ekman and Taylor read a Bakker epigraph's lexical markers - 'further argument', 'supposition', 'discourse' - as making the writing read like a philosophical treatise and implying a society that writes such treatises.
claims.source: Stefan Ekman and Audrey Isabel Taylor, JFA 32.2 (2021) 244-265
claims.quote: the writing suggests a philosophical treatise

claims.claim: Ekman and Taylor describe McKillip's chapter epigraph as written in the style of a scholarly treatise originating inside the fictional world, which sets itself up as an authoritative source.
claims.source: Stefan Ekman and Audrey Isabel Taylor, JFA 32.2 (2021) 244-265
claims.quote: The style is that of a scholarly treatise that emerges

claims.claim: Ekman and Taylor say an epigraph can settle which of epigraph and main text is the more reliable account, the scholarly or scientific epigraph making the main text read as the more biased one.
claims.source: Stefan Ekman and Audrey Isabel Taylor, JFA 32.2 (2021) 244-265
claims.quote: in which the epigraph is a more objective account

claims.claim: Ekman and Taylor say fictional epigraphs work by mimicking non-fiction text genres such as the research paper, the parliamentary debate and the historical treatise.
claims.source: Stefan Ekman and Audrey Isabel Taylor, JFA 32.2 (2021) 244-265
claims.quote: such as the research paper, the parliamentary debate, the historical

claims.claim: Lagus classifies Hobb's Ship of Magic as a pure figural narrative, formally like Martin's.
claims.source: Timo Lagus, 'Toward Figural Fantasy: The Representation of Consciousness in Modern American Fantasy Literature', MA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2006
claims.quote: a pure figural narrative formally similar

claims.claim: Lagus says Hobb, like Martin, uses consonant psychonarration and empathic free indirect discourse to great effect.
claims.source: Timo Lagus, MA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2006
claims.quote: uses consonant psychonarration and empathic FID to great effect

verdicts.trueWording: Two sentences use inverted syntax (the first and the last)
verdicts.note: Mythlore PDF p.63 (Wayback capture of dc.swosu.edu viewcontent; live PDF 403). Full sentence: 'Two sentences use inverted syntax (the first and the last), in addition to the parataxis across sentence boundaries ("And this is the thing") and the listing of parallel phrases ("a keenness of life, an uplifting of being"; "Compelling is this feeling [...] and addictive").' Preceded by 'the tonal dissonance of this passage is striking', which supports the 'drift' limb; Oliver's conclusion is that Fitz's personal experience leaks into the scholarly epigraph style.

verdicts.trueWording: this entire lengthy section is marked by the absence of a key detail
verdicts.note: Mythlore p.61. 'Thus, this entire lengthy section of narrative is marked by the absence of a key detail-Galen's tampering with Fitz's mind-a key detail that is nearly always present to the reader but never overtly stated.' The seventy-page limb is supported on the same page: 'Then Verity finally explicates what has been happening for the past 70 pages of the novel.' Both sentences refer to the same 'misted' section.

verdicts.trueWording: we are told what they are not doing, but it only leaves implied what they are doing
verdicts.note: Mythlore p.61. Context: the Skill breakthrough with Verity - 'And in that moment I realized we were not speaking aloud, and sat bolt upright and looked at him' (338). Oliver: 'What is striking about this sentence is that it does not explain what the breakthrough is: we are told what they are not doing, but it only leaves implied what they are doing (speaking using the Skill).' Both men (Fitz and Verity) and the magic-returns limb are supported.

verdicts.trueWording: training the reader to see what is not there, to imagine the connections
verdicts.note: Mythlore p.62. 'Thus, we could see this entire section of the novel as training the reader to see what is not there, to imagine the connections, the same mental process required of the historian constructing a narrative of the past based on evidence.' 'Supply the connections' = 'imagine the connections'.

verdicts.trueWording: recollection and gossip masquerading as an accurate description of the past
verdicts.note: Mythlore p.63, block quotation of Mendlesohn (16), attributed 'Mendlesohn's argument that this novel (and other epic fantasy like it) assumes...'; Works Cited confirms 'Mendlesohn, Farah. Rhetorics of Fantasy. Wesleyan UP, 2008.' Quote verbatim: 'Each chapter begins with a memoir not dissimilar to the Venerable Bede's history: recollection and gossip masquerading as an accurate description of the past.' Fair-reading caveat, not a defect: Mendlesohn calls the circular argument 'nonetheless valid', and Oliver replies that she 'misses how the structure of epigraph and negative space precisely draw attention to the "masquerade", undermining its authority even as it is instated' (p.64) - so the disputing-authority gloss is Oliver's reading of her as much as hers.

verdicts.trueWording: The conjunction 'but' here violates the conventional separation
verdicts.note: Mythlore p.55. 'Thus, in the second chapter, Fitz follows up a historical narrative in the epigraph by starting the main text with "But family rumor says" (24). The conjunction "but" here violates the conventional separation of epigraph from text, drawing attention to that relation rather than allowing the paratext to function invisibly.' Chapter-two and the 'But' limbs both explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: Chapter 22 has an inexplicable narrative intrusion into the epigraphs
verdicts.note: Mythlore p.62. 'Chapter 20 has epigraph text from the subjective perspective of another culture while the "objective" scholarly attribution is relocated to the main text at the start of the chapter, and Chapter 22 has an inexplicable narrative intrusion into the epigraphs, as the epigraph describes a dream-vision Fitz has'. Both named breaches verbatim. Context caveat, not an unsupported limb: Oliver introduces them as part of 'several instances' of heightened blurring and calls the chapter-15 epigraph 'the best example', so 'two' is not an exhaustive count of the breaches he records.

verdicts.trueWording: Naming customs, titles, and social positions, and what text genres exist
verdicts.note: Ekman & Taylor, JFA 32.2, p.253, 'Function Two: Adding Details' (Wayback raw capture of the DiVA PDF; live diva-portal.org timed out twice, curl exit 28). 'The epigraph source, as well as the epigraph itself, can provide information that indicates a way to approach a secondary world. Naming customs, titles, and social positions, and what text genres exist in the world can be determined from the sources given.' Note the page says the source AND the epigraph itself provide this; the claim's narrower 'source line' reading is still covered by 'can be determined from the sources given'.

verdicts.trueWording: Even without reading the texts of the epigraphs, it is possible to determine
verdicts.note: Ekman & Taylor p.253. Cherryh 'Gate of Ivrel' example, three source lines only: 'Even without reading the texts of the epigraphs, it is possible to determine that the secondary world contains a conflict between science and tradition, suggesting that mix of genres sometimes referred to as "science fantasy."' Generalized in the next sentence: 'Regardless of how the text portrays the world, the epigraph points out the generic context in which the world should be constructed for analysis.'

verdicts.trueWording: the writing suggests a philosophical treatise and thus hints at a form of society
verdicts.note: Ekman & Taylor p.252, on the Bakker epigraph (Ajencis, Discourse on War). 'Through linguistic markers such as "further argument," "supposition," and "discourse," the writing suggests a philosophical treatise and thus hints at a form of society in which such treatises are written.' All three lexical markers verbatim; 'linguistic markers' rather than 'lexical markers'.

verdicts.trueWording: The style is that of a scholarly treatise that emerges from within the fictional world
verdicts.note: Ekman & Taylor p.256, 'Function Three: Adding Perspectives', on McKillip's The Bards of Bone Plain chapter-two epigraph. Continues: 'The text sets itself up as an authoritative source while at the same time suggesting that the poems, ballads, and tales by or about Nairn do not convey a true picture.' Both limbs verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: in which the epigraph is a more objective account ... the main text is more biased
verdicts.note: Ekman & Taylor p.256. 'Epigraphs can determine the reliability of the main text (or its narrator) by either implying that the epigraph is the less reliable retelling (a ballad, prophesy, or tale for instance) and the main text is a more reliable version of events; or vice versa, in which the epigraph is a more objective account (for instance a scholarly or even scientific text) and the main text is more biased.'

verdicts.trueWording: mimicking text genres that are not fiction, such as the research paper, the parliamentary debate, the historical treatise
verdicts.note: Ekman & Taylor p.258. 'The epigraphs are parts of the work of fiction while mimicking text genres that are not fiction, such as the research paper, the parliamentary debate, the historical treatise. Their many voices can thus rely on both polyphony and mimicry to build a more complex world.' Sentence is scoped to McKillip's, Fforde's and Erikson's epigraphs, but the mimicry mechanism is stated generally.

verdicts.trueWording: Ship of Magic (1998) is a pure figural narrative formally similar to Martin's
verdicts.note: Lagus thesis, helda.helsinki.fi PDF fetched live (200, 143pp). Printed p.125 (PDF page 127): 'By comparison, Robin Hobb's (1952-) Ship of Magic (1998) is a pure figural narrative formally similar to Martin's. Its internal focalization is immersive and often pronounced, and its strong figurality is on a par with the figurality in Martin and Donaldson.' Metadata correction only, no bearing on the claim: p.125 sits in section 4.3 ('From the 1980s to the 2000s', pp.116-131), not ch. 5 (Conclusion, p.134).

verdicts.trueWording: Like Martin, Hobb uses consonant psychonarration and empathic FID to great effect
verdicts.note: Lagus, printed p.125, the sentence immediately following the claim-103 passage: 'Like Martin, Hobb uses consonant psychonarration and empathic FID to great effect. External focalization ... is negligible.' Lagus defines FID as free indirect discourse at 3.1/1.5. Same metadata correction as 103: the passage is in section 4.3, not ch. 5.
